expect:
Students may include:
• The 1922 Fordney–McCumber Tariff raised average import duties on manufactured goods by around 38%, making foreign products expensive and encouraging Americans to buy from US factories.
• This protection meant domestic firms could maintain higher prices and profits, fuelling investment in new plant and machinery.
• Mellon cut the top rate of income tax from 73% in 1921 to 25% by 1925, leaving wealthy investors with billions more to channel into shares and corporate bonds.
• These freed funds drove the Wall Street boom; share prices rose steeply across the decade as the demand for stocks outpaced new issues.
• A side effect was inequality: high tariffs and low income tax rewarded shareholders far more than wage earners or farmers, who faced higher prices for everyday goods and shrinking export markets — a problem covered in Lesson 2.

expect:
Students may include:
• The case combined three of the decade’s defining tensions in a single trial: fear of communism (Red Scare), prejudice against Italian-Americans, and the move towards immigration restriction.
• The 1921 conviction rested on thin and contradictory evidence; the trial judge, Webster Thayer, openly described the defendants as ‘anarchist bastards’, suggesting bias rather than impartiality.
• Their seven-year appeal and 1927 execution provoked international protests — rallies in Paris, London and Berlin showed how an American local trial had become a global symbol.
• Civil-liberties campaigners (including the new ACLU, founded 1920) used the case to argue that the Red Scare had eroded due process — an argument that long outlasted the trial.
• In 1977, fifty years after their execution, Massachusetts Governor Michael Dukakis issued a posthumous proclamation acknowledging the unfair trial.
• The case is named in the AQA spec because it concentrates the divisions of 1920s America in one event — a useful reference for any 8-mark or 12-mark question on the period.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of significance covering links to multiple 1920s themes and importance over time.
Secure: Clear explanation of why the case mattered.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to retelling the story.
Emerging: Describes the trial without explaining its significance.

Students may include:
• Stopped the banking panic — the four-day bank holiday closed every bank for inspection; only those judged solvent reopened on 13 March, and around $1 billion of cash flooded back into deposits within a fortnight.

expect:
Students may include:
• Banking rescue: the Emergency Banking Act (9 March 1933) closed banks for inspection; reopening triggered $1 billion of redeposits; Glass-Steagall (June 1933) created the FDIC insuring savings up to $5,000.
• Farm rescue: the AAA (May 1933) paid farmers to cut production; six million pigs slaughtered; farm income rose around 50% within two years.
• Mass relief: FERA distributed $500 million through Harry Hopkins; CCC employed 2.5 million young men by 1942 at $30/month; CCC built 800 state parks and planted three billion trees.
• Industrial recovery: NRA codes on wages, hours and prices; blue eagle symbol; 2.5 million employers signed up. PWA $3.3 billion built the Hoover Dam, Lincoln Tunnel, Triborough Bridge.
• Regional reform: TVA built 20 dams in seven southern states, brought electricity to over half the valley by 1940 and controlled flooding.
• Communication: fireside chats turned the presidency into a daily presence in 60 million radio homes.
• Limits: 11 million still unemployed in 1934; the New Deal cushioned but did not end the Depression; the Supreme Court later struck down NRA (1935) and AAA (1936).
• Conclusion: the First New Deal’s major impact was political and psychological as well as economic — it stopped the collapse, rebuilt confidence and redrew the role of the federal government in American life, even though full recovery would have to wait for the war.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

Students may include:

• Equal Pay Act (June 1963), signed by Kennedy: banned wage discrimination on grounds of sex.

• Title IX (1972): banned sex discrimination in any federally funded education programme; transformative for women’s sport, science and graduate study.

• Roe v Wade (January 1973): legalised abortion across the United States.
• Reform-minded presidents: Kennedy (Equal Pay Act), Johnson (Title VII), Nixon (signed Title IX).
• Conclusion: the legal victories combined writers and organisations naming the problem (Friedan, NOW), allies in the federal government during a reform decade, and Supreme Court rulings extending civil-rights logic from race to sex. The defeat of the ERA and the lasting controversy over Roe show the limits of the same period.
